https://www.theyeshivaworld.com/news/gen.text: Magnificent Budapest Synagogue Seized by the Nazis and Communists Reopens [PHOTOS] September 22, 2026 8:55 pm 2 Comments Eighty-two years after the sound of prayer that once echoed through its vast walls was forcibly silenced by the Nazis and their local collaborators, and 100 years after it was first established, the historic Rákospalota Synagogue in Budapest’s 15th District has returned to Jewish hands. In a moving and impressive ceremony held on the eve of Yom Kippur, attended by hundreds of Hungarian Jews and dozens of descendants of its founder, Rabbi Michael-Yitzhak Dushinsky, the beautifully restored synagogue was formally rededicated. On Yom Kippur itself, prayers were held there, with dozens of local Jews arriving with emotion to pray on the holiest day of the Jewish calendar. The story of the seized synagogue did not end with the horrors of the Holocaust. Following Hungary’s liberation from the Germans, the country came under Soviet rule, and the magnificent synagogue was turned into a storage facility for the Hungarian National Library. For decades, hundreds of thousands of books and newspapers were stored inside the building. The process of returning the synagogue to its original sacred purpose began approximately four years ago, when Hungary’s Chief Rabbi, Rabbi Shlomo Köves, began working to restore the building to Jewish use. Following lengthy negotiations, the process was completed, and within less than a year the synagogue underwent an extensive renovation, costing millions of euros. The restoration sought to preserve the building’s historic character and original decorative elements as faithfully as possible. The decorations were restored with, among other tools, the assistance of artificial intelligence, which helped enhance the only surviving interior photograph showing the synagogue in its former glory. Using this image as a reference, dozens of experienced professionals worked to recreate the interior as accurately as possible. The renovation was made possible with the generous support of philanthropist Igor Tolshinsky, who has been deeply involved in supporting Jewish community life in Hungary. At the heart of the rededication ceremony was the introduction of a new Torah scroll into the restored synagogue, symbolizing the revival of Jewish life. Prayers, singing and dancing filled the building, where for decades books had been stacked in the very place where Torah scrolls once stood. Among those attending the ceremony were the head of the Budapest rabbinical court and Chief Chabad emissary, Rabbi Baruch Oberlander; rabbis of Budapest synagogues and Chabad emissaries; philanthropist Igor Tolshinsky; Hungary’s government official responsible for religious affairs, István Szti; and other dignitaries. One of the most moving moments of the event was the arrival of 80-year-old Rabbi Michael Dushinsky, grandson of the synagogue’s founder, after whom the synagogue was also named, accompanied by numerous other members of the family. The rabbis formally appointed Rabbi Eli Nograd, a Chabad emissary, as the synagogue’s new rabbi and spiritual leader. Rabbi Nograd donned a tallit, recited the Shehecheyanu blessing with God’s name and kingship, and delivered an enthusiastic and emotional address to the participants. “The story of Rákospalota is, in many ways, a reflection of the story of Hungarian Jewry in recent decades: a building established during a period of flourishing Jewish life, which endured the destruction of the Holocaust, lost its original purpose for decades—and now returns to serve precisely the purpose for which it was built,” Rabbi Nograd said. The event took on added significance as the historic synagogue became the sixth to return to Jewish use as part of a broader initiative led by Rabbi Köves to revive historic synagogues across Budapest. “Am Yisrael Chai—the Jewish people live. For the local Jewish community, this is not merely the renovation of a historic building, but the restoration of a place that for decades stood as a symbol of a Jewish world that had disappeared, transforming it once again into an active center of prayer, Torah study and community life.
